{{Short description|Linear algebra concept}}
{{refimprove|date=February 2014}}
In [[linear algebra]], a '''semi-orthogonal matrix''' is a non-[[square matrix|square]] [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] with [[real number|real]] entries where: if the number of columns exceeds the number of rows, then the rows are [[orthonormal vectors]]; but if the number of rows exceeds the number of columns, then the columns are orthonormal vectors.


== Properties ==
Let <math>A</math> be an <math>m \times n</math> semi-orthogonal matrix.
* Either <math>A^{\operatorname{T}} A = I \text{ or } A A^{\operatorname{T}} = I. \,</math><ref>Abadir, K.M., Magnus, J.R. (2005). Matrix Algebra. Cambridge University Press.</ref><ref>Zhang, Xian-Da. (2017). Matrix analysis and applications. Cambridge University Press.</ref><ref>Povey, Daniel, et al. (2018). [http://dx.doi.org/10.21437/Interspeech.2018-1417 "Semi-Orthogonal Low-Rank Matrix Factorization for Deep Neural Networks."] Interspeech.</ref>
* A semi-orthogonal matrix is an [[isometry]]. This means that it preserves the norm either in row space, or column space.
* A semi-orthogonal matrix always has full rank. 
* A square matrix is semi-orthogonal if and only if it is an [[orthogonal matrix]].
* A real matrix is semi-orthogonal if and only if its non-zero [[singular value]]s are all equal to 1.
* A semi-orthogonal matrix ''A'' is [[semi-unitary]] (either ''A''<sup>†</sup>''A''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''I'' or ''AA''<sup>†</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''I'') and either left-invertible or right-invertible (left-invertible if it has more rows than columns, otherwise right invertible).
 

== Examples ==

=== Tall matrix (sub-isometry) ===
Consider the <math>3 \times 2</math> matrix whose columns are orthonormal:
<math>A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}</math>
Here, its columns are orthonormal. Therefore, it is semi-orthogonal, which is confirmed by:
<math>A^T A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I_2</math>

=== Short matrix ===
Consider the <math>2 \times 3</math> matrix whose rows are orthonormal:
<math>B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}</math>
Here, its rows are orthonormal. Therefore, it is semi-orthogonal, which is confirmed by:
<math>B B^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I_2</math>

=== Non-example ===
The following <math>3 \times 2</math> matrix has orthogonal, but not orthonormal, columns and is therefore not semi-orthogonal:
<math>C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}</math>
The calculation confirms this:
<math>C^T C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \neq I_2</math>

== Proofs ==

=== Preservation of Norm ===
If a matrix <math>A</math> is tall or square (<math>m \ge n</math>), its semi-orthogonality implies <math>A^T A = I_n</math>. For any vector <math>x \in \mathbb{R}^n</math>, <math>A</math> preserves its norm:
<math>\|Ax\|_2^2 = (Ax)^T(Ax) = x^T A^T A x = x^T I_n x = \|x\|_2^2</math>
If a matrix <math>A</math> is short (<math>m < n</math>), it preserves the norm of vectors in its [[Row and column spaces|row space]].

=== Justification for Full Rank ===
If <math>A^T A = I_n</math>, then the columns of <math>A</math> are linearly independent, so the rank of <math>A</math> must be <math>n</math>.
If <math>A A^T = I_m</math>, then the rows of <math>A</math> are linearly independent, so the rank of <math>A</math> must be <math>m</math>.
In both cases, the matrix has full rank.

=== Singular Value Property ===
The statement is that a real matrix <math>A</math> is semi-orthogonal if and only if all of its non-zero singular values are 1.

:This follows directly from the [[Singular Value Decomposition|SVD]], <math>A = U \Sigma V^T</math>.

:(<math>\implies</math>) Assume <math>A</math> is semi-orthogonal. Then either <math>A^T A = I</math> or <math>A A^T = I</math>. The non-zero singular values of <math>A</math> are the square roots of the non-zero eigenvalues of both <math>A^T A</math> and <math>A A^T</math>. Since one of these "Gramian" matrices is an [[identity matrix]], its eigenvalues are all 1. Thus, the non-zero singular values of <math>A</math> must be 1.

:(<math>\Leftarrow</math>) Assume all non-zero singular values of <math>A</math> are 1. This forces the block of <math>\Sigma</math> containing the non-zero values to be an identity matrix. This structure ensures that either <math>\Sigma^T \Sigma = I_n</math> (if <math>A</math> has full column rank) or <math>\Sigma \Sigma^T = I_m</math> (if <math>A</math> has full row rank). Substituting this into the expressions for <math>A^T A = V(\Sigma^T \Sigma)V^T</math> or <math>A A^T = U(\Sigma \Sigma^T)U^T</math> respectively shows that one of them must simplify to an identity matrix, satisfying the definition of a semi-orthogonal matrix.
